# Coleman llms.txt

> Generated file. Do not edit manually.
> Source: scripts/generate_llms_txt.py

## Project

Coleman is a framework for test-case prioritization in CI using multi-armed bandits,
with typed YAML configuration, deterministic run identifiers, sweep orchestration,
parallel execution, and extensibility via hooks and namespaced custom config.

### FILE: README.md

# COLEMAN

**Adaptive CI test prioritization, from 37 bandit policies to reproducible experiments and auditable evidence.**

[![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-start_here-4051b5)](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/)
[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.14%2B-blue)](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green)](LICENSE)

[![Tests](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/codecov.yml/badge.svg?branch=main&event=push)](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/codecov.yml?query=branch%3Amain)
[![Configured coverage gate: 95%](https://img.shields.io/badge/coverage_gate-95%25-brightgreen)](docs/quality-and-security.md#tests-and-coverage)
[![Sonar vulnerabilities](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs&metric=vulnerabilities)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/overall?id=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs)
[![Sonar security rating](https://sonarcloud.io/api/project_badges/measure?project=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs&metric=security_rating)](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/overall?id=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs)

[![Dependency advisory audit](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/security-audit.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/security-audit.yml)
[![Lint and NumPy parameter documentation](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/pylint.yml/badge.svg?event=pull_request)](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/pylint.yml?query=event%3Apull_request)
[![Complexity and maintainability](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/code-cost.yml/badge.svg?event=pull_request)](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/code-cost.yml?query=event%3Apull_request)
[![Documentation build](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/docs.yml/badge.svg?branch=main&event=push)](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/docs.yml?query=branch%3Amain)

Your test suite changes, failures are rare, and the CI budget is finite. COLEMAN
brings adaptive ranking, budgeted test replay, configurable-system testing and
evidence-based comparison into one Python platform. Choose a policy, learn from
execution feedback, explore its parameters and inspect the resulting test order,
fault-detection quality and modeled execution cost.

The approach is grounded in the [original TCPCI study](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2020.2992428)
(**IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, TSE**), the
[SPLC configurable-software study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3382025.3414967)
and its [Empirical Software Engineering extension](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-021-10093-3).

Since these studies, COLEMAN has evolved into a reusable **CI Intelligence
platform**. It now combines [37 policies](#mab-policies-available),
[parameter sweeps](#sweep-engine), [source-to-Parquet workflows](#datasets),
resumable checkpoints and [protected comparisons](docs/protected-evaluation.md)
with [versioned result records](docs/domain-results.md) and explicit
[provenance](#provenance). **TCPCI remains its core.**

The platform connects **source data → reproducible experiments → inspectable
results → evidence for a decision**. Use it as a Python library or through the CLI;
Parquet results and local checkpoints work without external services.

**Follow the experiment from decision to resource cost.** Query results with
DuckDB or Polars, persist native results in ClickHouse, and watch progress,
ranking latency, CPU and memory through the optional OpenTelemetry → Prometheus →
Grafana stack. [Explore results and monitoring](#results-and-live-observability).

[Run your first experiment](#quick-start) · [Explore the policies](#mab-policies-available) ·
[Choose a dataset](#datasets) · [Read the research](#research-background) ·
[Inspect quality and security](#quality-you-can-inspect) · [Contribute](CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Quality you can inspect

Research software should make its engineering evidence inspectable too. COLEMAN
enforces a **configured 95% combined line/branch coverage gate**, checks complexity and
maintainability, audits every locked dependency, and publishes **Sigstore-signed
distributions with a CycloneDX SBOM**. Follow the checks to inspect their actual
scope and results:

| Engineering commitment | Verification and evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Test behavior and recovery | [Python 3.14 test suite](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/codecov.yml): unit/integration tests, versioned golden fixtures, deterministic identities, interrupted writes, checkpoint continuation and import boundaries; a failed configured coverage gate fails the run |
| Audit known dependency vulnerabilities | [Lock-wide advisory audit](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/security-audit.yml): runtime and optional/development packages across platforms, on dependency changes, weekly and on demand; queried pins and JSON results are retained |
| Review dependency changes | [License and vulnerability review](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/dependency-review.yml) on pull requests, alongside Dependabot updates and [security reporting](SECURITY.md) |
| Inspect source and credentials | [SonarCloud analysis](https://sonarcloud.io/summary/overall?id=jacksonpradolima_coleman4hcs) and GitGuardian PR checks; inspect the individual check results for the proposed commit |
| Keep code and API documentation consistent | [Ruff lint/format and NumPy parameter checks](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/pylint.yml) at the documented public entry points |
| Bound structural complexity | [Xenon and Radon gates](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/code-cost.yml): block/module/average limits C/B/A and maintainability index ≥20 |
| Keep human and machine documentation usable | [Strict documentation builds](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/docs.yml) and [deterministic `llms.txt` verification](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/llms-txt.yml) |
| Measure the installed implementation | [Decision observations](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/decision-benchmarks.yml): bounded correctness/performance profiles from an installed wheel, outside the checkout; manual runs and an opt-in weekly schedule |
| Make releases inspectable | [Published wheel, sdist, Sigstore bundles and SBOM](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/latest), produced with locked tooling by the [release workflow](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/actions/workflows/release.yml) |

The [quality and security guide](docs/quality-and-security.md) explains how to read
the badges, reproduce checks and verify release artifacts. The coverage badge
states the enforced threshold; current measured coverage is in the test log.
Additional local qualification covers typing, docstring presence and
installed-package examples. Engineering checks complement the
[scientific comparison protocol](docs/evaluation-guide.md).

## One platform, connected workflows

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[COLEMAN: adaptive CI test prioritization]
    C --> D[Prepare test histories]
    C --> E[Run budgeted experiments]
    C --> V[Evaluate the evidence]
    C --> O[Study CI integration]
    D --> E
    E --> V
    V --> O
    R[Research and explicit assumptions] --> D
    R --> V
```

## What you can build with COLEMAN

| Your goal | Available workflow |
| --- | --- |
| Compare adaptive CI prioritization policies | The native TCPCI runner, [37 policies](#mab-policies-available), RNFail/TimeRank rewards, contextual inputs and [parameter sweeps](#sweep-engine) |
| Watch experiments while they run | [Provisioned Grafana dashboards](docs/observability.md#watch-a-run): active executions, cycle progress, NAPFD/APFDc, checkpoint activity and ranking/evaluation latency |
| Understand the framework's resource footprint | [Persisted CPU and memory samples](docs/observability.md#understand-resource-measurements), plus [Scalene and py-spy profiling](docs/code-cost.md) for investigating hotspots |
| Query results with your analytical tools | [Parquet, embedded DuckDB or optional ClickHouse](#results-and-live-observability), SQL and Polars analysis, with configuration and provenance retained locally |
| Stress a difficult CI decision | [32 deterministic interaction-covering cases](docs/ci-stress-laboratory.md), explicit truth and feedback clocks, native Parquet and resumable agents |
| Audit what a source actually supports | [Source admission](docs/corpus-admission.md): original evidence, explicit units and a 35-axis production-reality matrix |
| Compare repeated CI experiments | [Raw build/seed records and paired repository-family means](docs/corpus-evaluation.md), explicit missingness and protected access |
| Compare metrics with known limits | [Conservative bounded paired means](docs/bounded-paired-evaluation.md), full-family uncertainty and practical equivalence under declared independent-unit assumptions |
| Assess public CI collection | [Bounded public Actions collection](docs/public-ci-feasibility.md), typed receipts and reality-axis accounting that retains missing test and physical-cost evidence |
| Develop comparable baseline matrices | [Frozen native-policy and heuristic matrices](docs/comparable-baselines.md), explicit incompatibilities, raw costs and checkpoint recovery |
| Evaluate configurable software | [Original LibSSH → WTS/VTS Parquet and checkpointed replay](docs/hcs-parquet-etl.md), [CTest corroboration](docs/hcs-trace-evidence.md) and [whole-set/variant strategies](docs/highly-configurable.md) |
| Collect real-fault observations | [Controlled Java matrices](docs/java-fault-matrix.md) and [Python source capture](docs/python-source-capture.md), pinned source/runtime recipes, raw process evidence and offline recovery |
| Inspect a constructed C weakness | [Pinned Juliet/GCC capture](docs/c-seeded-source-capture.md), an independent arithmetic oracle, raw process evidence and interruption recovery |
| Reproduce and inspect an experiment | [Typed RunSpec and the library API](#library-api), [configuration identity and provenance](#provenance), Parquet results and resumable checkpoints |
| Select finite coverage under a budget | [Coverage selection](docs/finite-coverage.md), explicit costs and solver-specific certificates and limits |
| Allocate resources under declared scenarios | [Scenario-payoff allocation](docs/scenario-payoffs.md), signed outcomes, resource constraints and conservative evidence handling |
| Check a CI decision before adoption | [Independent mathematical benchmarks](docs/decision-benchmarks.md), [protected comparisons](docs/protected-evaluation.md) and [operational accounting](docs/operational-pilot.md) |
| Extend or integrate the platform | [Library API](#library-api), [application API and optional MCP](docs/application-api.md), [versioned domain results](docs/domain-results.md), hooks and [runner extensions](docs/extensibility.md) |
| Tune an experiment and return to it later | [Durable experiment workflows](docs/durable-experiments.md): typed Random/UCB plans, bounded grids, native checkpoint recovery and a separate audited evaluation stage; requires this source revision's wheel |

The workflows retain their own assumptions: a source conversion, controlled fault,
mathematical check and historical policy comparison answer different questions.
Follow the linked guide for a complete example and the evidence it supports.

## MAB policies available

**37 selectable policies** cover simple comparators, confidence bounds, Bayesian
sampling, changing histories, contextual features, subsets, pairwise rankings and
policy portfolios. These are the actual native configuration names:

| Family | Available policies |
| --- | --- |
| Random and greedy | `Random`, `Greedy`, `EpsilonGreedy`, `DecayEpsilonGreedy`, `OptimisticGreedy`, `EpsilonDecreasing` |
| Confidence-based exploration | `UCB`, `UCB1`, `UCB2`, `KLUCB`, `UCBTuned`, `UCBV`, `MOSSUCB` |
| Bayesian and stochastic exploration | `ThompsonSampling`, `BayesianUCB`, `BootstrappedThompson`, `Softmax`, `Pursuit`, `PHE` |
| Adversarial exploration | `EXP3`, `EXP3IX` |
| Changing histories and recent feedback | `SlidingWindowUCB`, `DiscountedUCB`, `ChangeDetectionUCB`, `FRRMAB`, `SlMAB` |
| Contextual | `LinUCB`, `SWLinUCB`, `LinTS`, `SWLinTS`, `ContextualEpsilonGreedy`, `SWContextualEpsilonGreedy` |
| Combinatorial | `CombinatorialUCB`, `CombinatorialThompson` |
| Dueling and ranking | `DuelingUCB`, `PairwiseThompsonRanking` |
| Portfolio meta-policy | `PortfolioUCB` |

Use the [policy guide](docs/policies.md) to understand the families, reward choices,
required parameters and contextual feature availability. The
[constructor reference](docs/api/policy.md) gives the exact API; configuration packs
cover a subset of the policies. The [baseline workflow](docs/comparable-baselines.md)
adds history-based heuristic comparators under a declared common protocol.

The original [bandit analysis](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1013689704352),
[LinUCB study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0146) and
[combinatorial framework](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/chen13a.html) explain
important foundations. A policy name alone does not establish that a CI adaptation
satisfies the original theorem's assumptions or outperforms the simple comparators.

## Quick start

Use Python 3.14+ in a virtual environment. This command pins a published wheel
and verifies its SHA-256 before installation:

```bash
python -m pip install "https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.19.1/coleman-4.19.1-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=ca470ba2be14ca755952f0bb3bc92615d76b90f95ebdd41dc1cdc9847713cc93"
```

### Library API

Save the following as `first_run.py` in an empty directory. It creates a tiny
authored history, runs the actual Random and UCB policies, and prints the result
directory. Durations in this example are seconds; the data demonstrates a mechanism.

```python
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from coleman.api import run
from coleman.spec import RunSpec

dataset = Path("data/example-ci")
dataset.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
rows = [
    {"BuildId": build, "Name": name, "Duration": duration,
     "CalcPrio": 0, "LastRun": "2026-01-01", "Verdict": verdict}
    for build in (1, 2, 3)
    for name, duration, verdict in (
        ("unit", 1.0, 0), ("integration", 2.0, build % 2), ("system", 4.0, 0)
    )
]
pl.DataFrame(rows).write_parquet(dataset / "features-engineered.parquet")

spec = RunSpec.model_validate({
    "execution": {"independent_executions": 1, "parallel_pool_size": 1, "seed": 42},
    "experiment": {
        "datasets_dir": "data", "datasets": ["example-ci"],
        "policies": ["Random", "UCB"], "rewards": ["RNFail"],
        "budget": {"mode": "ratio", "values": [0.5]},
    },
    "algorithm": {"ucb": {"rnfail": {"c": 1.0}}},
    "results": {"out_dir": "runs"},
    "checkpoint": {"enabled": True, "interval": 1},
})
result = run(spec)
print(result.run_id, result.artifacts_dir)
```

```bash
python first_run.py
```

The [complete tutorial](docs/getting-started.md) explains the output, queries it
with DuckDB, enables checkpoint continuation, and runs the same experiment from
YAML. The [configuration reference](docs/configuration.md) covers packs and sweeps.

## Sweep engine

Compare UCB exploration settings without writing another execution loop. After
the example above, reuse its `spec` and append this code to `first_run.py`:

```python
from coleman.api import run_many, sweep
from coleman.spec.sweep import SweepAxis, SweepSpec

base = spec.model_copy(deep=True)
base.experiment.policies = ["UCB"]
candidates = sweep(base, SweepSpec(
    axes=[SweepAxis(params={"algorithm.ucb.rnfail.c": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]})],
    seeds=[42, 43],
))
results = run_many(candidates, max_workers=1)
print(f"Completed {len(results)} UCB runs")
```

This expands three exploration settings × two seeds into six specifications,
each with its own run directory and checkpoint namespace. Grid and zip axes are
supported. Seeds repeat algorithmic randomness; use
[protected evaluation](docs/protected-evaluation.md) to separate parameter tuning
from evaluation and preserve the actual independent observation units.
See [configuration and CLI sweeps](docs/configuration.md) for complete YAML forms.

## Results and live observability

**Analyze the outcome and the cost of producing it.** COLEMAN records native CI
quality metrics alongside process CPU time, elapsed time and available memory
measurements. Keep experiments local, or connect the optional monitoring stack
when running longer experiments and parameter sweeps.

| Tool or workflow | What you can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Parquet + DuckDB / Polars** | Keep the default compressed, partitioned results; query build-level observations directly with SQL or DataFrames, with no database server |
| **Embedded DuckDB sink** | Select `results.sink: duckdb` to write a local `coleman_results` table; process workers use separate database files by default |
| **ClickHouse sink** | Select `results.sink: clickhouse` and install the `clickhouse` extra to send native result rows to a shared analytical database |
| **OpenTelemetry + Prometheus + Grafana** | Export native metrics, add trace instrumentation, inspect live progress, filter by dataset/execution/policy/budget, and follow CPU, RSS memory and latency in a provisioned dashboard |
| **Runtime profiling** | Investigate CPU and memory hotspots with the developer workflows for [Scalene and py-spy](docs/code-cost.md) |

After the [quick start](#quick-start), inspect the framework's recorded footprint
from the same directory:

```python
import duckdb

with duckdb.connect() as connection:
    print(connection.sql("""
        SELECT policy, COUNT(*) AS observations,
               MAX(process_memory_peak_rss_mib) AS process_peak_rss_mib,
               AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS mean_sampled_cpu_percent,
               MAX(process_cpu_time_seconds) AS sampled_cpu_seconds,
               MAX(wall_time_seconds) AS sampled_elapsed_seconds
        FROM read_parquet('runs/*/results/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
        GROUP BY policy
        ORDER BY policy
    """))
```

These are **COLEMAN process measurements**: CPU time and elapsed time accumulate
within an execution attempt; peak RSS is the process lifetime high-water mark.
Several policies can share a process, so grouping samples by policy does not
isolate that policy's resource cost. Unavailable readings remain `NULL`.
The [measurement guide](docs/observability.md#understand-resource-measurements)
explains platform support and sampling limits.

The [observability guide](docs/observability.md) connects a complete runnable
example to Docker Compose, dashboard filters, result-sink configuration and SQL.
Live telemetry complements stored results; [operational accounting](docs/operational-pilot.md)
and [resource replay](docs/resource-replay.md) address evidence about the subject
CI workload and its physical costs.

## Provenance

A run retains its resolved specification, configuration-derived identity,
environment provenance, Parquet results and enabled checkpoints. Inspect and query
them using the [first-run tutorial](docs/getting-started.md) and
[analysis playbook](docs/analysis-playbook.md). The run ID identifies configuration;
source-adapter receipts separately bind original input and output bytes.

For extensions and integrations, [versioned measurement records](docs/domain-results.md)
retain units, semantics, logical identity, provenance and explicit missing states.
[Point-in-time observations](docs/point-in-time-observations.md) preserve what was
available at each decision even after late results or corrections arrive.
The [architecture guide](docs/setup.md) explains how these contracts connect to
the runner, result sinks, telemetry and artifact publication.

## Datasets

Choose the evidence type as well as the file format. Runnable data is useful
before it qualifies for a claim about effectiveness in historical or future CI.

| Source or laboratory | Usable workflow | Evidence scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [LRTS: Karaf, ActiveMQ, Log4j](docs/lrts-parquet-etl.md) | Original Jenkins reports → analytical/native Parquet → checkpointed replay; [separate stage views](docs/lrts-stage-views.md) | Historical observations with explicit post-hoc replay assumptions |
| [RTPTorrent: HikariCP](docs/rtptorrent-parquet-etl.md) | Verified ZIP64 archive → class-level history → bounded native replay | Class observations; source chronology and admission gaps remain visible |
| [LibSSH](docs/hcs-parquet-etl.md) | Original CSV/JSON → WTS/VTS inputs → native replay; [original CTest corroboration](docs/hcs-trace-evidence.md) | Variant/attempt-aware source evidence, including missing cells |
| [Westermo](docs/westermo-parquet-etl.md) | Original embedded-system results → typed analytical Parquet | Preserves abnormal outcomes and unverified duration semantics |
| [Controlled Java](docs/java-fault-matrix.md), [Python](docs/python-source-capture.md), [C](docs/c-seeded-source-capture.md) | Pinned source/runtime → raw process evidence → offline validation | Controlled fault or constructed weakness observations |
| [CI stress laboratory](docs/ci-stress-laboratory.md) | Deterministic cases → known truth → native Parquet and replay | Constructed mechanism checks for drift, churn, rare failures and late feedback |
| Druid, Retrofit and Dune examples | Native/contextual/variant inputs in the checkout | Legacy examples with source-specific qualification limits |

The [dataset guide](docs/datasets.md) connects downloads, resource requirements,
licenses, adapters and the question each source can answer. A full admitted
historical cross-corpus confirmation has **not** been completed; see
[evidence status](docs/roadmap.md). Negative and inconclusive findings are valid results.

## Research background

COLEMAN (*Combinatorial VOlatiLE Multi-Armed BANdit*) originated in **test case
prioritization in continuous integration (TCPCI)** and expanded to highly
configurable software. Its scientific lineage
is directly connected to the workflows above:

| Original publication | Research contribution | Explore it in COLEMAN |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prado Lima and Vergilio. [*A Multi-Armed Bandit Approach for Test Case Prioritization in Continuous Integration Environments*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2020.2992428). **IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (TSE) 48(2), 453–465, 2022.** | Adaptive prioritization with feedback across changing CI test suites | [Bandit loop](docs/concepts.md), [policies](docs/policies.md), [experiments](docs/experiments.md) |
| Prado Lima, Mendonça, Vergilio and Assunção. [*Learning-based prioritization of test cases in continuous integration of highly-configurable software*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3382025.3414967). **SPLC, 2020.** | Learning-based prioritization in highly configurable software | [Whole-test-set and variant-test-set strategies](docs/highly-configurable.md) |
| The same authors. [*Cost-effective learning-based strategies for test case prioritization in continuous integration of highly-configurable software*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-021-10093-3). **Empirical Software Engineering 27, article 133, 2022.** | Extended evaluation of WTS/VTS across variants and budgets | [LibSSH data and replay](docs/hcs-parquet-etl.md), [original CTest evidence](docs/hcs-trace-evidence.md) |

The [research guide](docs/research.md) also connects the original algorithm,
dataset, data-leakage and statistical-method papers to their corresponding
features. Findings from an original study apply to its subjects and protocol;
later policies and datasets need their own comparable evaluation.

## Citation

Use [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff), or cite the original article:

```bibtex
@article{pradolima2022coleman,
  author = {Prado Lima, Jackson A. and Vergilio, Silvia Regina},
  title = {A Multi-Armed Bandit Approach for Test Case Prioritization in Continuous Integration Environments},
  journal = {IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering},
  year = {2022},
  volume = {48},
  number = {2},
  pages = {453--465},
  doi = {10.1109/TSE.2020.2992428}
}
```

## Contributing

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup, NumPy-style
docstrings, scientific conventions and review checks. The
[maintainability guide](docs/maintainability.md) explains the current architecture
and measured improvement priorities. Report vulnerabilities through
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). COLEMAN is distributed under the [MIT license](LICENSE).



### FILE: CONTRIBUTING.md

# Contribute to COLEMAN

Help make adaptive CI experiments understandable, reproducible and useful.
Contributions can improve a policy, a source adapter, an example, an explanation
or a contract. Begin with the user question and preserve the evidence behind the
answer.

For a tour of the product, start with the
[documentation map](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/).
For current architectural findings and improvement priorities, read
[maintainability](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/maintainability/).
The [quality and security guide](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/quality-and-security/)
maps automated gates, local qualification and release evidence to their actual scope.

## Set up a development checkout

Use Python 3.14+, uv and Git. From the cloned repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman.git
cd coleman
uv sync --frozen --extra dev --extra docs --extra telemetry --extra mcp --group build
uv run --frozen --no-sync pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type commit-msg --hook-type pre-push
```

This installs the locked development and documentation tools plus the extras used
by integration tests. Notebook, ClickHouse and controlled-capture work may need
additional extras or the exact runtime in that guide. `make install` provisions
the broader development environment; the DevContainer is an optional route with
its own monitoring services. Read its scripts before choosing that setup.

Create a focused branch from updated `main`. Keep source archives, raw capture
outputs and large datasets outside the Git worktree. Normal tests use small owned
fixtures and run without network access.

## Choose the right boundary

Reuse the runner, RunSpec, source cache, sinks, artifact writer and checkpoints.
A new source adapter should retain original meaning and publish an explicit native
projection, rather than introducing another experiment engine. Keep CLI, HTTP,
process execution and optional MCP dependencies at their adapter boundaries.

Extend typed models for contracted state. Do not pass undocumented dictionaries
through the application when a domain contract is needed. Preserve old data
meanings, schema readers, deterministic identities and golden artifacts. Unknown
versions should fail according to their contract; a migration must not invent
missing units or provenance.

See [architecture](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/setup/) and
[extensions](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/extensibility/) for concrete paths.

## Write useful NumPy-style docstrings

Public modules, classes and functions need docstrings. Document each public
parameter using NumPy's `Parameters` section, and describe return values and
meaningful errors. Document constructor parameters on the class or constructor.
Include units, invariants, missingness, side effects, concurrency and compatibility
where they affect use. A one-line description is not evidence that these are covered.

```python
import math


def observed_seconds(value: float) -> float:
    """Validate an observed elapsed duration.

    Parameters
    ----------
    value : float
        Finite, nonnegative elapsed duration in seconds. Zero is observed;
        unavailable duration must use the caller's explicit missing state.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        Validated elapsed seconds, without unit conversion or rounding.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the duration is negative or non-finite.

    Notes
    -----
    Performs no I/O and does not infer physical runner occupancy.
    """
    if not math.isfinite(value) or value < 0:
        raise ValueError("Duration must be finite and nonnegative")
    return value
```

This is a documentation pattern, not an additional SDK function.
Follow the [NumPy style guide](https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/stable/format.html).
Run `make docstrings` for the currently enforced public entry points. To inspect
the broader backlog without treating it as a passing global gate:

```bash
uv run --frozen --no-sync python scripts/audit_docstrings.py > /tmp/coleman-docstring-audit.json
```

The audit checks signature coverage without importing inspected code. It does not
certify parameter-description accuracy, complete return/exception documentation or
which exported names constitute a stable API. `interrogate` separately checks
whether docstrings exist.

## Write documentation as a connected path

Lead with the reader's goal and a complete working example. Explain prerequisites,
inputs, expected output and what to do next. Use the central map and topic hubs
instead of adding another top-level navigation item for each feature.

- Put tutorials in the experiment, data, evaluation or integration path.
- Keep exact schemas and symbol details in reference pages.
- Link the relevant original paper where a method or source is explained.
- Explain a paper's role without claiming it validates later extensions.
- Keep release chronology in the compatibility archive.
- Update diagrams when relationships change, and give graph links a plain-text alternative.
- Add NumPy docstrings when a tutorial exposes a previously undocumented parameter.

Build the site strictly, inspect the generated pages, run the example outside the
checkout against a built package, and regenerate `llms.txt`. Do not edit that
generated file by hand.

## Validate a change

```bash
make lint
make format-check
make typecheck
make interrogate
make docstrings
make cost-structural
make docs
uv run --frozen --no-sync python scripts/generate_llms_txt.py
uv run --frozen --no-sync python -m pytest
uv build --no-build-isolation
git diff --check
```

Use focused tests while developing; the full relevant suite and installed-package
checks qualify the final change. Prefer `python -m pytest` from the project
environment. If intentionally skipping the whole-project coverage gate for a
focused run, add `--no-cov`. The full suite retains multiprocessing/thread coverage,
branch measurement and its 95% minimum; instrumentation timings are not performance
benchmark results.

The structural limits are Xenon C for an individual block, B for a module and A
for the project average, plus maintainability index at least 20. Inspect the
reason for a hotspot before extracting helpers solely to change a score.
[Code-cost guidance](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/code-cost/)
explains structural and runtime measurements.

## Preserve scientific meaning

Keep negative, heterogeneous and inconclusive results. Seeds do not substitute for
independent observations. Preserve build/job/stage/variant/attempt grouping.
Distinguish raw outcomes, ranking scores, transformed rewards, calibrated
probabilities and inference. Compare sophisticated methods with simple baselines
under comparable source, budget, feedback and resource conditions.

Observed historical CI, controlled faults and synthetic mechanisms support
different claims. A successful conversion or a closed issue does not grant source
admission. When evidence is insufficient, report it and retain a conservative
fallback. The [evidence guide](https://jacksonpradolima.github.io/coleman/evaluation-guide/)
connects those rules to supported workflows.

## Submit a focused pull request

Use Conventional Commits, for example `docs: explain budgeted CI replay` or
`fix: reject conflicting source identities`. Explain the concrete problem,
resulting behavior, compatibility and validation in the PR description. Include
reproduction commands for source or behavior claims. Keep unrelated refactors out.

Before a maintainer push, review the whole diff from the merge-base. Use Alibaba
OpenCodeReview only in local delegation mode, read every applicable returned rule,
and manually review excluded tests and Markdown. Record file coverage and results;
fix confirmed critical, high and medium findings. Never configure an external
code-review endpoint for this workflow. Recheck the complete diff after material
changes, consolidate review fixes, and resolve valid threads with evidence.

A PR is ready to merge when required checks pass and blocking review findings are
resolved. Ordinary tests should not download external corpora or require a private
service. Installed-package tests should exercise the principal component outside
the checkout. Package and source identity checks matter when a producer fingerprints
its implementation; stage new package files before constructing the final wheel.

## Report a problem

For a bug, include the smallest reproducible input, command, expected/actual result,
OS, Python and package version, and relevant artifact identities. Preserve unknown
values and redact credentials. For a design proposal, explain the CI problem and
current limitation before suggesting a new abstraction.

Follow the [security policy](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for vulnerability reports. Contributions use the repository's
[MIT license](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/blob/main/LICENSE).



### FILE: docs/analysis-playbook.md

# Analysis Playbook

This guide is a complete reference for post-run analysis in Coleman, focused on
decision-quality, cost, stability, and extensibility impact.

Use this after one or more experiment runs have produced Parquet data under
your configured results directory.

## Protected comparisons

The summaries below are descriptive. For chronological eligibility, frozen
candidates, durable holdout access, paired independent-unit inference and
insufficient-evidence reports, use [protected evaluation](protected-evaluation.md).
Repeated seeds/worker executions do not increase the number of independent units.

## Data Access Patterns

### DuckDB (recommended)

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect("analysis.duckdb")
con.execute(
	"""
	CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW experiment_results AS
	SELECT *
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	"""
)
```

### Basic sanity checks

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total FROM experiment_results;

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT execution_id) AS executions,
	   COUNT(DISTINCT policy) AS policies,
	   COUNT(DISTINCT reward_function) AS rewards
FROM experiment_results;
```

## Core Comparisons

### 1. Quality ranking (NAPFD)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) AS std_napfd,
	   COUNT(*) AS n
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC;
```

### 2. Cost-aware quality ranking (APFDc)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(cost) AS std_apfdc,
	   COUNT(*) AS n
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY avg_apfdc DESC;
```

### 3. Stability (coefficient of variation)

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   reward_function,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) AS std_napfd,
	   CASE
		 WHEN AVG(fitness) = 0 THEN NULL
		 ELSE STDDEV_SAMP(fitness) / AVG(fitness)
	   END AS cv_napfd
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy, reward_function
ORDER BY cv_napfd ASC NULLS LAST;
```

## Budget and Scenario Sensitivity

Use scenario/time-ratio segmentation to find robust policies.

```sql
SELECT scenario,
	   policy,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc,
	   AVG(prioritization_time) AS avg_prioritization_time
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY scenario, policy
ORDER BY scenario, avg_napfd DESC;
```

If your scenario naming encodes time ratio, normalize it once and persist a
derived table for repeated analyses.

## Quality vs Cost Frontier (Pareto)

Goal: maximize NAPFD and APFDc. The legacy `cost` column contains an APFDc
quality score; it is not execution expense in seconds or money.

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

df = duckdb.sql(
	"""
	SELECT policy,
		   reward_function,
		   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd,
		   AVG(cost) AS avg_apfdc
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	GROUP BY policy, reward_function
	"""
).df()

def pareto_frontier(data: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
	pts = data.sort_values(["avg_apfdc", "avg_napfd"], ascending=[False, False]).reset_index(drop=True)
	keep = []
	best_napfd = float("-inf")
	for _, row in pts.iterrows():
		if row["avg_napfd"] > best_napfd:
			keep.append(True)
			best_napfd = row["avg_napfd"]
		else:
			keep.append(False)
	return pts.loc[keep].copy()

front = pareto_frontier(df)
print(front)
```

Interpretation:

1. Points on the frontier are non-dominated trade-offs.
2. Off-frontier points are strictly worse in both metrics than at least one alternative.

## Win Rate Analysis (Pairwise)

Compare how often one policy beats another on the same execution slice.

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

base = duckdb.sql(
	"""
	SELECT scenario,
		   execution_id,
		   policy,
		   AVG(fitness) AS score
	FROM read_parquet('./runs/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=1)
	GROUP BY scenario, execution_id, policy
	"""
).df()

pivot = base.pivot_table(index=["scenario", "execution_id"], columns="policy", values="score")
policies = list(pivot.columns)

rows = []
for a in policies:
	for b in policies:
		if a == b:
			continue
		valid = pivot[[a, b]].dropna()
		wins = (valid[a] > valid[b]).sum()
		total = len(valid)
		rows.append({"policy_a": a, "policy_b": b, "win_rate": wins / total if total else None, "n": total})

win_rate_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values(["policy_a", "win_rate"], ascending=[True, False])
print(win_rate_df.head(30))
```

## Runtime and Resource Footprint

```sql
SELECT policy,
	   AVG(prioritization_time) AS avg_prioritization_time,
	   AVG(process_memory_rss_mib) AS avg_rss_mib,
	   AVG(process_cpu_utilization_percent) AS avg_cpu_pct,
	   AVG(fitness) AS avg_napfd
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY policy
ORDER BY avg_prioritization_time ASC;
```

Use this to identify policies that are fast enough for CI budget constraints.

## Extensions and Hook Artifacts

When using runner hooks and extensions, persist additional artifacts under the
run folder (for example, JSON/CSV derived from custom domain logic).

Recommended pattern:

1. Write one artifact per execution_id.
2. Include run_id, dataset_id, execution_id, and worker_id in each record.
3. Join artifact rows with experiment results in DuckDB for impact analysis.

Example join pattern (adapt paths to your artifact layout):

```sql
WITH base AS (
  SELECT run_id, execution_id, policy, fitness, cost
  FROM experiment_results
),
ext AS (
  SELECT run_id, execution_id, custom_signal, custom_bucket
  FROM read_json_auto('./runs/**/artifacts/*.json')
)
SELECT b.policy,
	   e.custom_bucket,
	   AVG(b.fitness) AS avg_napfd,
	   AVG(b.cost) AS avg_apfdc
FROM base b
JOIN ext e
  ON b.run_id = e.run_id AND b.execution_id = e.execution_id
GROUP BY b.policy, e.custom_bucket
ORDER BY avg_napfd DESC;
```

## Reproducibility Checklist

1. Keep spec.resolved.json and provenance.json for every run.
2. Compare only runs with consistent datasets and time-ratio sets.
3. Report both central tendency and variance.
4. Track run_id and execution_id in every exported table/chart.
5. Version-control analysis scripts and generated figures metadata.

## Suggested Reporting Bundle

For each experiment campaign, export:

1. Overall ranking by NAPFD and APFDc.
2. Pareto frontier table and scatter chart.
3. Stability table (std and CV).
4. Scenario sensitivity matrix.
5. Runtime/resource table.
6. Hook/extension impact table (if enabled).

## Continue the workflow

Use the [evaluation guide](evaluation-guide.md) to separate descriptive plots from justified
comparisons, then explore the [workflow notebook](workflow.md) for a complete operational example.

### FILE: docs/api/evaluation.md

# Evaluation

Coleman includes classic TCP/IR-aligned metrics:

- NAPFD and NAPFD-Verdict
- APFDc
- Precision@k
- Recall@k
- AveragePrecision@k (AP@k)
- ReciprocalRank@k (RR@k, equivalent to MRR for a single ranked suite)
- NDCG@k (normalized discounted gain at top-k)

Literature references:

- Rothermel, G.; Untch, R. H.; Chu, C.; Harrold, M. J. (2001). Prioritizing test cases for regression testing. IEEE TSE.
- Elbaum, S.; Malishevsky, A. G.; Rothermel, G. (2002). Test case prioritization: a family of empirical studies. IEEE TSE.
- Catal, C.; Mishra, D.; Tufekci, S.; Cagiltay, N. E. (2011). Mapping study of software test case prioritization. Software Quality Journal.
- Manning, C. D.; Raghavan, P.; Schutze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press.
- Baeza-Yates, R.; Ribeiro-Neto, B. (2011). Modern Information Retrieval (2nd ed.). Addison-Wesley.
- Thakur, N.; Reimers, N.; Ruckle, A.; et al. (2021). BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks.
- Muennighoff, N.; Tazi, N.; Magne, L.; Reimers, N. (2023). MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. EACL.

::: coleman.evaluation

# Source materialization API

Use `SourceCache` and a frozen `MaterializationSpec` to verify permitted source
bytes and selected archive members. Network readers are explicit adapters;
validation works offline. Materialization does not grant scientific admission.

Start with [the source-cache workflow](../corpus-materialization.md) or choose a
[dataset adapter](../datasets.md). The docstrings below describe byte bounds,
side effects, errors and concurrency limits.

# Measurement record API

Use `DomainRecord` when an extension needs raw observations with explicit units,
semantics, missingness and provenance. Native `fitness`/`cost` result columns
retain their original contract; they are not migrated implicitly into this one.

compatibility rules, then [evaluation](../evaluation-guide.md) for interpretation.

::: coleman.results.domain



### FILE: docs/api/reward.md

# Reward

Coleman supports reward formulations inspired by TCP, ranking, and cost-aware literature:

- RNFail (binary fault signal)
- TimeRank (failure-aware order-sensitive reward)
- ReciprocalRank (inverse-rank gain)
- TopKRNFail (prefix-constrained binary reward; precision-style)
- DiscountedFailure (DCG-like logarithmic discount)
- APFDc (cost-aware reward using execution time and detected failure positions)

Literature references:

- Spieker, H.; Gotlieb, A.; Marijan, D.; Mossige, M. (2017). Reinforcement Learning for Automatic Test Case Prioritization and Selection in Continuous Integration. ISSTA.
- Jarvelin, K.; Kekalainen, J. (2002). Cumulated gain-based evaluation of IR techniques. ACM TOIS.
- Rothermel, G.; Untch, R. H.; Chu, C.; Harrold, M. J. (2001). Prioritizing test cases for regression testing. IEEE TSE.
- Elbaum, S.; Malishevsky, A. G.; Rothermel, G. (2002). Test case prioritization: a family of empirical studies. IEEE TSE.
- Manning, C. D.; Raghavan, P.; Schutze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press.

::: coleman.reward

### FILE: docs/application-api.md

# Bounded CI application API and optional MCP

For configurable Random/UCB tuning, persistent jobs and conversational recovery,
start with [durable experiment workflows](durable-experiments.md). That opt-in
workspace uses a separate versioned contract. This page documents the original
seven ephemeral tools and their compatibility boundaries.

Expose bounded CI operations through shared application services. The application layer makes its existing
native services available through reusable, bounded commands. It does not introduce a new runner,
an LLM decision algorithm, or a hosted service.

## Install the release

Use Python 3.14 or later on Linux or macOS in an activated virtual environment:

```bash
python -m pip install 'https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.17.0/coleman-4.17.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=e5a272ddc0edf72bd909a743fa2b3bc0dfeb8a02871c487ab22683cddeea40ca'
```

For optional tools, install the same GitHub wheel with its extra:

```bash
python -m pip install 'coleman[mcp] @ https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/download/v4.17.0/coleman-4.17.0-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=e5a272ddc0edf72bd909a743fa2b3bc0dfeb8a02871c487ab22683cddeea40ca'
```

Use this repository's release assets and verify their published digest and
attestations. The bare PyPI name belongs to a different project. Base CLI/library
execution requires no MCP dependency, model, credentials, network service, or
client. The optional adapter is tested against the pinned MCP Python SDK 2.3.0
and its negotiated MCP protocol; the independent COLEMAN application contract is
`coleman-application-v1`.
Contributor `make install` includes the optional SDK to exercise its tests and
type annotations; installing the base release wheel still excludes it.

## Architecture and ownership

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Library[Typed library commands] --> Service[ApplicationService]
    CLI[coleman application] --> Commands[Versioned command boundary]
    MCP[Optional local MCP stdio tools] --> Commands
    Commands --> Service
    Registry[Host-approved immutable registry] --> Service
    Identity[Trusted caller context] --> Service
    Service --> Queue[Bounded queue and lifecycle supervisor]
    Queue --> Worker[Owned subprocess with deadline and resource guards]
    Worker --> Coverage[Native finite coverage solver]
    Worker --> Allocation[Native scenario allocation service]
    Worker --> Runner[Existing api.run and TCPCI runner]
    Coverage --> Publish[Existing ArtifactWriter: complete immutable JSON]
    Allocation --> Publish
    Runner --> Publish
    Publish --> Receipt[Schema-validated caller-owned result handle]
    Receipt --> Portable[Explicit portable export and import]
```

Domain packages never import CLI or MCP. Native `run`, sweeps, extensions, sinks,
checkpoints and unrestricted library APIs retain their existing behavior. The
application service owns a unique private session directory under a trusted
host-selected root. Clients select registered IDs; they cannot send a RunSpec,
plugin import, path, shell command, dataset URL or exporter endpoint.

The packaged registry contains three **synthetic smoke fixtures**:

| Spec ID | Native service | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `weighted-overlap-3` | Finite coverage | Overlapping A/B/C capabilities, modeled duration in seconds |
| `signed-ci-resource-3` | Scenario allocation | Declared joint scenario model with conservative evidence handling |
| `native-ci-smoke-v1` | TCPCI runner | Two synthetic builds, Random baseline, RNFail, seed 42, fixed-time budget 3 s |

These fixtures validate integration and mathematics; they are not independent
CI observations or evidence of practical time savings. Seeds do not create
independent observations. Native allocation retains its insufficient-evidence
and conservative fallback semantics.

## Complete library example

Run from outside the checkout after installing the wheel:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from coleman.application import (
    ApplicationService, Caller, Parameters, ResultBundle, Submit, default_registry,
)
from coleman.selection import CoverageResult

caller = Caller(subject="local-analysis")  # supplied by trusted host code
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    with ApplicationService(default_registry(), root=Path(directory)) as service:
        print(service.capabilities().to_json())
        request = Submit(
            schema_version=1,
            request_id="ci-budget-3",
            spec_id="weighted-overlap-3",
            parameters=Parameters(budget=3),
        )
        initial = service.submit(request, caller=caller)
        final = service.wait(initial.job_id, caller=caller)
        assert final.state == "completed" and final.handle is not None
        bundle = service.result(final.handle, caller=caller)
        assert isinstance(bundle.result, CoverageResult)
        assert bundle.result.selected_ids == ("A", "C")
        assert bundle.result.cost.value == 3
        assert bundle.result.objective.value == 1
        assert service.submit(request, caller=caller).job_id == final.job_id
        exported = service.export_result(final.handle, caller=caller)
        Path(directory, "portable.json").write_text(exported, encoding="utf-8")
        assert ResultBundle.from_json(exported) == bundle
        imported = service.import_result(exported, caller=caller)
        assert imported.handle is not None
        assert imported.handle.digest == final.handle.digest
```

Save the export outside a temporary directory to retain it after shutdown.
Coverage budget overrides are exact nonnegative decimals, at most twelve decimal
places, in the registered cost unit and meaning. JSON serializes them as decimal
strings. Zero is valid; null means **no override**. Negative budgets, non-finite
values, unknown keys and implicit unit conversions are rejected. Allocation and
experiment parameters are frozen in their registrations in v1.
Application JSON readers preserve decimal number literals before precision
validation, so extra digits cannot disappear through intermediate binary64
rounding. Existing native readers retain their original compatibility behavior.

One-shot CLI execution uses the same command and services:

```bash
coleman application --request '{"schema_version":1,"request_id":"ci-budget-3","spec_id":"weighted-overlap-3","parameters":{"budget":3}}'
coleman application --request '{"schema_version":1,"request_id":"native-ci","spec_id":"native-ci-smoke-v1"}'
```

CLI output is a canonical JSON envelope. Success contains `ok: true` and `data`;
errors contain `ok: false`, a stable `error` and safe human `message`. A failed or
expired one-shot job returns the same error envelope, includes its typed state
in `data`, and exits with status 2. Existing
`coleman run --config ...` remains available.

## Native experiment registration by trusted hosts

For your own approved local dataset, create a normal RunSpec in host code, set
one sequential worker, one to sixteen executions and an explicit seed; use the
Random baseline, one or two RNFail/TimeRank rewards, and one to eight budgets.
Disable checkpoints, telemetry, hooks and extensions; use the local Parquet sink.
Call `register_experiment("approved-ci", spec)` and pass the returned immutable
`Configuration` to `ApplicationService`. Registration snapshots up to eight
`<datasets_dir>/<dataset>/features-engineered.parquet` files, totaling 1 MiB, with
at most 10,000 rows per dataset and 1,000 candidates per build. Dataset IDs use
the conservative application ID alphabet. This bounded adapter deliberately
supports a smaller surface than unrestricted native RunSpec execution.
The seed and every repetition offset (`seed + iteration_index`) must fit the
unsigned 64-bit range shared by the native NumPy/Polars execution path. Negative
seeds and overflowing repetition ranges are rejected during registration.

Inputs are copied into an owned worker directory; original files are never
reread during execution. Normalized relative input/output paths make the native
resolved run ID independent of temporary directories. Configuration fingerprints
bind complete input bytes and normalized RunSpec. Work units are total builds ×
executions × rewards × budget values. An over-limit experiment is rejected before
queue admission; work-limited decisions can return an explicitly limited native
result. V1 does not resume application jobs through native checkpoints. Existing
direct checkpoint APIs remain available separately.

Registration recomputes build/candidate dimensions from the snapshotted bytes.
The bounded adapter requires integer build IDs and binary verdicts, unique
testcase names per build, numeric finite nonnegative durations in seconds and
non-null native required columns. Invalid rows are rejected; this adapter never
invokes the legacy loader's null-duration-to-zero coercion. The direct legacy
loader remains compatible with its existing callers. Algorithm overrides are
outside the approved Random baseline registration surface in v1.
Build IDs must also survive the native loader's signed Int64 conversion; values
outside that range are rejected before execution.
Registration also checks the actual native duration conversion (Float64 loader
then the bandit's Float32 schema): overflow and positive-to-zero underflow are
rejected. Genuine zero and representable subnormal durations remain valid;
ordinary native rounding is preserved and native result bytes keep that meaning.
Budget values must produce unique native directory segments of at most 255 UTF-8
bytes. This also rejects different ratio budgets rounded to the same native label;
existing unrestricted native naming remains unchanged.
`CalcPrio` must be an integer column fitting the bandit's signed Int32 schema.
`LastRun` must survive the existing string conversion; unsupported nested values
are refused. Duration validation applies the loader's Float64 conversion first,
so supported decimal/integer source columns retain their native behavior.

Experiment bundles contain original resolved-specification and native result
bytes with logical filenames, byte counts, SHA-256 and canonical base64.
`provenance.json` in a produced bundle is explicitly a
`portable-native-provenance-v1` derivative: it records schema version, COLEMAN
producer/version, Python/platform runtime facts, the original local file's
SHA-256, and the redacted field names `cwd`, `git`, `uv_lock_hash`. Ambient host
directories, Git context and lock-file context are not exported. The original
native provenance file remains unchanged inside the worker until cleanup;
the source digest permits host-side audit and does not authenticate a producer.
Import preserves supplied evidence and never extracts files. Existing Parquet fields retain their
legacy meanings; unavailable metrics are not invented or converted to zero.
Runtime observations, timestamps and native shard filenames can differ across
equivalent executions. Mathematical results and approved-source provenance are
compared separately from runtime metadata and complete artifact digests.

## Limits, states and failures

`Limits` requests are reduced componentwise by `ServerPolicy.caps` before work.
Default caps are 30 elapsed seconds including queue/startup, 10,000 native work
units, 100 candidates, 512 MiB worker peak RSS/solver allocation ceiling and
256 KiB combined native output files plus portable result JSON. Native solver working-memory estimates cap at
1 GiB even if a host permits larger worker RSS. Native proof/dimension ceilings
still apply. The service defaults to one active worker, eight pending jobs,
64 retained job identities, 16 MiB reserved results and 2 GiB reserved active
worker memory. Limits count bytes, seconds and documented native work units;
they are not calibrated probabilities or scientific quality guarantees.

Admission reserves each job's maximum output until expiry and sums admitted
worker memory before starting processes. Registry snapshots are bounded to 32
configurations of 1.5 MiB each. Parent/interpreter overhead, input snapshots,
protocol frames and temporary serialization buffers add bounded local overhead
outside worker RSS. Linux worker peak RSS uses the current executable's kernel
`VmHWM`, because `getrusage` can include the parent's footprint before `exec`.
Other platforms retain the existing sampler; historical general telemetry and
stored artifacts keep their existing meaning. The memory ceiling is unchanged.
Worker RSS and native-file output are checked before/after
calculation and sampled every 20 ms; transient overshoot is possible. Unsupported
RSS measurement fails closed. This is a guard for trusted local native code,
not a hard memory allocator or hostile-code sandbox. The underlying SDK stdio
framing is for a trusted local client and is not an untrusted network ingress
limit. Hosted deployment needs its own authenticated, size/concurrency-limited
gateway and process/resource isolation; v1 provides none.
Pending admission counts actual capacity after active memory reservations:
unused concurrency slots do not expand the pending queue when memory prevents
their use. Jobs that fit an available slot start before `submit` returns;
otherwise the finite pending-queue cap applies. A zero queue cap permits only
immediate starts. Portable evidence imports require storage, not a worker slot.

Completion retains only the validated portable JSON bundle. Native work files,
input copies and private request files are removed after the worker exits, before
the completed receipt is issued; the bundle preserves native result/specification
bytes and the explicit redacted provenance derivative. Retained output reservations therefore cover the entire completed job
directory. Before final publication, the combined native-file and bundle byte
count must also fit the admitted output cap.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued: validated and admitted
    queued --> running: worker and memory slot
    queued --> cancelled: cancel wins
    queued --> failed: worker startup fails
    queued --> expired: elapsed deadline
    running --> completed: exit zero and validated immutable JSON
    running --> failed: native error or resource refusal
    running --> cancelled: cancel wins
    running --> expired: elapsed deadline
    completed --> expired: retention TTL
    failed --> expired: retention TTL
    cancelled --> expired: retention TTL
```

Cancellation and completion commit under the same lock: the first terminal state
wins. Cancelling a completed job returns completion unchanged; cancelling queued
or running work terminates/reaps its worker and exposes no partial result. A
complete native incumbent with a work-limit status is valid evidence, not an
optimality claim. Native failures never become fabricated negative scientific
results. Only exit zero plus valid, matching native result JSON permits completion.

Retention starts at a terminal state, defaults to one hour, and deletes result
bytes on expiry. Status retains an `expired` tombstone; retrieval returns the
stable expiry error. Request IDs are scoped by trusted caller: identical retries
reuse the same job, changed commands conflict, and expired IDs never silently
start new work. Tombstones count toward the finite session job limit. After that
limit, start a new service session deliberately. `close()` cancels work and removes
session files. Restart loses job handles; orphaned crash directories require
trusted operator cleanup. Export/import is the explicit portable continuation,
not a claim to resume an interrupted native calculation.

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `invalid_input` | Invalid schema/version/parameter, changed request ID or wrong issued digest |
| `unknown_spec` | No such approved configuration |
| `not_found` | Job absent from this service session |
| `forbidden` | Existing job belongs to a different trusted caller |
| `expired` | Deadline or result retention expired |
| `resource_limit` | Input, native workload, queue, job, output or memory limit |
| `unavailable_result` | No completed result, corrupted artifact, worker failure or closed session |

Status is inspectable before a handle exists. A handle includes schema version,
job ID and content digest. Ownership is checked independently **before** exposing
its result. A digest proves integrity, not producer identity or authorization.
Imports recheck decision mathematics and opaque experiment-file hashes, then issue a fresh local
handle to the importing caller; they do not attest the claimed producer or run
any imported content. Imported experiment observations remain producer claims,
not independently rerun evidence. Bundle v1 requires integer version 1; missing, future and
unknown versions fail closed. Legacy native artifacts keep their existing readers;
there is no automatic migration or reinterpretation.

## Configure MCP once, then use tools

After installing the optional wheel extra, point an MCP-capable local client at
the absolute executable `/tmp/coleman-application-env/bin/coleman-mcp`, with no
arguments. This starts a local stdio server with the packaged registry. A trusted
custom host can instead call `create_server(service, caller=...)` with its own
approved registry. Each process has one host-owned local principal; caller fields
inside requests are rejected. There is no HTTP listener or hosted authentication.

Once configured, the client can discover configurations, submit a bounded CI
request, poll status, cancel, retrieve and export/import results through tools.
The user does not run a shell command for each request. No model is required to
exercise these operations; a natural-language client is only another consumer.

| Tool | Argument | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `discover` | none | IDs, kinds, fingerprints, budget units/meaning, policy and submit JSON schema |
| `submit` | `request_json` | Versioned `JobView` in success envelope |
| `status` / `cancel` | `command_json`: `{"schema_version":1,"job_id":"..."}` | Job state |
| `result` / `export_result` | `handle_json`: exact issued handle | Portable bundle in `data` |
| `import_result` | `bundle_json`: serialized exported `data` | New local completed job and handle |

Commands have a 16 KiB cap before JSON parsing; imports use the server output
cap. MCP JSON framing and escaping add overhead to the bundle byte cap. Unknown
fields, duplicate JSON keys, traversal/import/URL attempts and future versions
fail before execution. Standard SDK protocol/schema failures remain MCP errors;
valid tool invocations return the versioned COLEMAN success/error envelope.

The no-model tests use the actual optional SDK client both in process and over
stdio, then repeat the stdio lifecycle from an installed noneditable wheel outside
the checkout. They also verify base installation without MCP, real two-build
native execution, CLI/library/tool mathematics, caller isolation, races, immutable
publication, golden fixtures, portability, expiry, malicious inputs and saturation.

## Continue the workflow

Choose your integration boundary in the [integration guide](integration-guide.md), or return to the
[native experiment API](api/experiment-api.md) when a registered application session is unnecessary.



### FILE: docs/benchmark-corpus.md

# Versioned CI benchmark corpus: foundation and local profiles

Use versioned manifests, a typed registry and descriptive data cards to inspect
what a CI source contains. Bounded correctness fixtures, native profiles,
[verified materialization](corpus-materialization.md) and
[source admission](corpus-admission.md) connect source identity to explicit limits.
Start with the [dataset guide](datasets.md) for a complete runnable source path.

[Comparable baselines](comparable-baselines.md) and
[repeated observations](corpus-evaluation.md) reuse those identities while keeping
raw attempts, source exclusions and repository-family grouping visible.
[Westermo analytical Parquet](westermo-parquet-etl.md) provides another original
source view without inventing duration units or historical availability.

The [historical corpus phase was closed with unmet criteria](roadmap.md#historical-corpus-status).
Its delivered workflows remain usable at their declared scopes; the final
historical cross-corpus confirmation was not completed. Original registry and
phase-one fixture-readiness meanings are unchanged.

## Installed commands

Install the wheel attached to [COLEMAN 4.17](https://github.com/jacksonpradolima/coleman/releases/tag/v4.17.0)
in a Python 3.14+ environment, or build a development wheel from the reviewed source.
Copy examples to a directory outside the checkout. Once installed, these local
operations need no optional dependency, provider subscription, credential or
network access.

```bash
python -m coleman.corpus list
python -m coleman.corpus show ci-serial-boundary-v1
python -m coleman.corpus schema
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-serial-boundary-v1 --output corpus-artifacts
python -m coleman.corpus validate ci-parallel-occupancy-v1 --output corpus-artifacts
```

`list` returns registered IDs, explicit blocked reasons, verified fixture IDs
(empty until validation evidence is supplied), and all missing minimum regimes.
`show` returns the complete typed card. `schema` emits the manifest's structural
JSON schema; semantic cross-field checks still require the library validator.
`validate` writes a deterministic immutable report and returns its path/source
digest. Exit 0 means the requested metadata or tiny correctness operation passed;
it does not mean corpus diversity is satisfied. Invalid/blocked sources, unknown
IDs, future schemas, unsupported adapters, bad bytes or output failures return 2.
CLI output must remain within the current workspace; existing symlinked report
parents are resolved and checked before publication. This local path check assumes
no concurrent hostile filesystem mutation; it is not an OS sandbox. Library callers
supply their own trusted `ArtifactWriter` root, independently of CLI/MCP transports.

The profile commands below and [source-package validation](corpus-materialization.md)
provide shared foundations. Follow the [dataset adapters](datasets.md),
[stress laboratory](ci-stress-laboratory.md), [baseline matrices](comparable-baselines.md)
and [evaluation guide](evaluation-guide.md) for their implemented workflows.
The final historical confirmation remains [unfinished](roadmap.md#historical-corpus-status).

## Source contract and admission

The [RTPTorrent source assessment](rtptorrent.md) in COLEMAN 4.5 adds a
bounded raw-class reader and an owned isolated native replay. It preserves repeated
class executions and missing CI clocks; it does not admit an external source or
change the registry's diversity inventory.

The [LRTS source assessment](lrts.md) preserves processed metadata alongside raw
Jenkins method/suite/node identities. Its bounded owned replay checks native
compatibility; missing availability, stage mapping and expected-suite evidence
keep real-source temporal evaluation blocked.

`CorpusManifest` schema v1 binds:

- source URI/version/citation, SHA-256, byte count and verified local availability;
- specific data license ID, terms URI/digest/review time and redistribution rule;
- adapter/version and its actual implementation state;
- logical observation/group dimensions and shared source dependence group;
- event, outcome and feature availability fields, timestamp origin and timezone;
- explicit verdict mapping, failing-test versus genuinely mapped fault unit,
  duration units/meaning and unknown-outcome policy;
- intended evaluation purpose, temporal boundaries when available, budget units,
  budgets, seed labels, metrics and source resource limits;
- input/output row counts and unique primary exclusion reasons with conservation;
- validity limitations that remain visible in human and machine reports.

Registration is not admission. `blocking_reasons` exposes unresolved prerequisites;
`require_ready()` checks metadata only. `validate_fixture_source()` additionally
checks real bytes, canonical source grammar, actual row counts, declared field
semantics and native correctness. A metadata declaration is a producer attestation,
not cryptographic proof of legal rights, completeness or statistical independence.

Fixture reports embed their parsed source data. Their validation, reads and
publication therefore require `redistribution="permitted"`. Verified `recipe_only`
terms can support metadata registration or future download recipes, but cannot
authorize an embedded-source fixture report through the library API.

The phase-one adapter supports only `ci-fixture-json`, version `1`, for constructed
synthetic correctness inputs. It never imports an adapter from a user-provided
name or follows its URI. Other formats remain visible registrations with planned
adapters. In particular, native Parquet inputs are not silently routed through
legacy missing-value coercions: the new admission gate must establish semantics
before those inputs can enter a corpus evaluation. Direct native behavior is
unchanged.

Data cards retain facts separately from claims: observed footer row counts and
source byte counts are available in the inventory; unverified duration profiles
are unavailable. Null language/execution axes are unverified; empty axes are
explicitly inapplicable to a purely numerical fixture. Constructed/control
histories cannot be labeled observed CI, and synthetic fixtures cannot be labeled
real faults. Seeded-fault and controlled-real-fault layers must retain matching
seeded/real origins or explicitly unverified origin; contradictory classifications
fail when registering or serializing cards. Context/variant artifacts retain shared
dependence groups rather than becoming additional independent projects.

The initial inventory pins the exact public source revision
`b743f51d5ba444410b32f2c0e318b2587b882c43`; every file's SHA-256, byte size and Parquet
footer row count were checked against that Git object. It contains 1,386,730
source rows across ten artifacts, **not** that many independent observations.
Physical duration/churn/availability/provider semantics remain unverified, not zero.
The local profiling recipe below describes raw fields without resolving those gates.

## Local profiles and the first diversity matrix (4.4)

These additions are available in the 4.4 wheel; 4.3 and older wheels retain their
previous commands. The profiler is a separate descriptive recipe, **not** an implemented corpus evaluation adapter.
It does not change registry v1, cards, fixture/readiness v1, old native result
rows, source licenses or admission blockers.

```bash
# SOURCE is a local copy of the exact registered file, not a download URL.
python -m coleman.corpus profile native-example-e970afe1686d7fe6 source.parquet --output profiles
# Copy examples/corpus-profiles/inventory.py outside the checkout first.
python inventory.py /absolute/path/to/coleman corpus-inventory
```

The inventory example reads the ten existing files from the explicit checkout,
checks every frozen digest/size, and publishes ten profiles plus one complete
inventory. It fetches nothing, copies no source data and runs no evaluation.
A missing, changed or oversized source prevents publication of a complete new
inventory. Existing completed inventories remain content-addressed evidence of
their original inputs; failed later invocations do not erase them.

The pinned source snapshot produces this matrix. Contextual files and separately
stored variants can share the same executions; these rows must not be added as
independent projects. Execution groups retain `Variant` when present, whereas
logical builds count `BuildId` among rows with complete group identity.

| Registered artifact | Raw rows | Logical builds | Execution groups | Repeated identity rows | Conflicting identities | Failed rows | Raw Duration median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Druid | 308998 | 168 | 168 | 0 | 0 | 237 | 0.002 |
| Druid contextual | 308998 | 168 | 168 | 0 | 0 | 237 | 0.002 |
| Retrofit | 71238 | 2711 | 2711 | 0 | 0 | 161 | 0.196 |
| Retrofit contextual | 71238 | 2711 | 2711 | 0 | 0 | 161 | 0.196 |
| Dune Debian 10 | 119316 | 1029 | 1029 | 4433 | 3237 | 1417 | 0.07 |
| Dune Ubuntu 20.04 | 44052 | 367 | 367 | 1408 | 1031 | 532 | 0.09 |
| Dune Debian 11 | 35140 | 290 | 290 | 1291 | 886 | 193 | 0.03 |
| Dune total | 229213 | 2186 | 2186 | 6689 | 4858 | 3094 | 0.3 |
| Dune variants | 198508 | 1036 | 1686 | 7132 | 5154 | 2142 | 0.07 |
| Synthetic example | 29 | 5 | 5 | 0 | 0 | 14 | 0.134 |

Raw `Duration` medians have **unverified source units**, not seconds. They are not
comparable across sources and cannot be used to infer runner work, parallel wall
time or savings. Failed rows use only the explicitly declared binary failing-test
mapping with exact native-type comparisons, without rounding decimal labels to
binary64; they are not unique faults. Repeated identity rows count rows beyond
the first complete declared observation key. A conflicting identity has multiple
`(Duration, Verdict)` pairs. These are integrity findings, not deduplicated or
resolved outcomes. Different context values alone are outside that conflict test.

Every profile includes all source column names/null counts, raw duration finite,
null, nonfinite, negative and zero counts, min/median/p95/max, raw verdict categories,
missing identity/group counts, and the distribution of raw rows per execution
group. The latter includes duplicates and is not a count of distinct runnable
tests. Quantiles use the inverse empirical CDF `ceil(p*n)-1`, without interpolation,
over finite binary64 values. Quantile ranks use integer arithmetic; signed zeros
normalize to positive zero in statistical projections while source bytes/digests
remain unchanged. All-null/nonfinite or empty distributions have null
quantiles and unavailable measurements; observed zero stays zero. Negative raw
numbers remain visible and do not certify valid physical execution durations.
A declared duration unit/meaning is retained when supplied; it is never guessed.

Chronology is explicitly **not evaluated** by this recipe. `LastRun`, numeric
`BuildId`, file order and repeated seeds cannot establish event order, UTC,
feature/outcome availability, time span, adjacent-build churn, flakiness, retries
or independent observations. These facts and provider/language axes remain
unverified where their original cards lack evidence. All **seven regimes remain
uncovered**; profiles cannot promote a source or weaken that diversity matrix.

This complete library example uses the same exact local synthetic file as the CLI:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from coleman.artifacts import ArtifactWriter
from coleman.corpus import (
    CorpusProfileInventory, NativeSourceProfile, load_registry,
    profile_native_source, publish_profile_inventory, publish_source_profile,
)

registry = load_registry()
card = registry.card("native-example-e970afe1686d7fe6")
profile = profile_native_source(card, Path("source.parquet"))
assert profile.rows == 29 and profile.logical_builds == 5
assert profile.raw_duration.zero_count == 3
assert profile.duration_median.unit == "source-unit-unverified"
assert profile.card == card  # No admission metadata is rewritten.
writer = ArtifactWriter("library-profiles")
path = publish_source_profile(profile, writer)
assert NativeSourceProfile.from_json(path.read_bytes()) == profile
inventory = CorpusProfileInventory(
    schema_version=1, registry=registry, profiles=(profile, profile),
    uncovered_required_regimes=registry.required_regimes,
)
assert len(inventory.profiles) == 1  # Identical retries are idempotent.
assert len(inventory.uncovered_required_regimes) == 7
publish_profile_inventory(inventory, writer)
```

The default ceiling is 16 MiB compressed input, two million rows, 64 columns and
256 MiB declared uncompressed row-group bytes; tighter manifest bounds also apply.
One bounded byte snapshot is hashed before decoding. Footer limits precede native
Parquet decoding, but are not measured peak-memory guarantees or a sandbox for
malicious codecs. Inputs are explicit trusted local files. Source URI strings
never trigger downloads or dynamic imports. Numeric summaries are descriptive
producer attestations: reading validates conservation, membership, sign counts
against inverse-CDF quantile ranks, equality at shared ranks, and integral
group-count quantiles consistent with the total rows. Nonempty complete group
rows require logical builds and execution groups. Key-column null counts bound
missing identities/groups, and
duplicates require original identities covering the known build/group grain.
Observed source-row/byte declarations must agree with the profile; the declared
row/source-byte resource ceilings also apply on reads. Without `Variant`, logical
builds and execution groups are equal. Missing group/observation identities retain
their subset relationships and extra-column null bounds. Reproducing the
producer's observations still requires the matching source and recipe.

New `NativeSourceProfile` and `CorpusProfileInventory` schema-v1 artifacts use
`corpus-profiles/` and `corpus-profile-inventories/`; native manifests discover both.
Missing, duplicate-key, future or unknown versions fail closed. There is no implicit
migration from old native artifacts/cards into profile evidence. Recompute from
reviewed source bytes and preserve the old artifact alongside the new family.
Identical publication and interrupted retry reuse existing immutable artifacts;
a completed profile is published only after its complete source scan. Profiling
has no incremental learning state and needs no second checkpoint store.

## Independent known answers

The serial source has t1=1 s/pass, t2=2 s/fail, t3=4 s/fail, base order t1/t2/t3.
Every excluded known failing test stays in the denominator.

| Budget | Selected | Failing-test recall | NAPFD | APFDc | First failure | Runner work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 runner-s | t1, t2 | 1/2 | 1/4 | 5/14 | 3 elapsed-s | 3 runner-s |
| 7 runner-s | t1, t2, t3 | 1 | 1/3 (full-suite APFD) | 1/2 | 3 elapsed-s | 7 runner-s |

APFDc here names the native **full-universe cost** convention, including excluded
failures and full-suite duration. It is a normalized ordering/selection measure,
not financial cost. It cannot be substituted for an unrelated selected-only cost
formula. No unique-fault recall is inferred from binary test verdicts.

The parallel fixture dispatches all three tests at zero on three distinct workers:
**7 runner-seconds, 4 elapsed-seconds, first failure at 2 seconds**. No serial
APFD/APFDc value is inferred for that schedule. Queue, shared setup and overhead
are not modeled or claimed saved.

Hand-declared source answers are checked against separate exact `Fraction`/tick
references, then the real native `NAPFDVerdictMetric` or existing event replay is
checked against those answers. The exact oracle imports no production metric or
scheduler. Its scope is at most 16 complete binary tests. The native fixture
projection uses integer seconds <=1,000,000 to preserve exact input costs in
Float32/Float64; this is a fixture restriction, not a generic unit conversion.
Actual scalar checking declares binary64 absolute tolerance `1e-12`, with zero
relative tolerance. Exact rational answers remain authoritative in the source.

Zero is real. No failure detected gives null/right-censored time; a failure at
